title: spaceNEXT 2026 | Advancing U.S. Space Commerce: Policy Frameworks for Global Leadership
transcriptText:
As you heard in the introduction, yes, I
work in the US Office of Space Commerce.
And what I want to talk about today
really is first just to briefly
introduce you to the office because I
think even though we're playing an
increasingly important role in the US
government and broader space ecosystem,
not everyone knows what we do, but then
also really dive down into a particular
problem set that we are heavily focused
on on the policy side. So first in terms
of what the office is, we sit inside the
department of commerce and we we have
three primary missions. One is we have a
small regulatory office. We regulate the
commercial remote sensing industry. So
companies including many in the DMV
region that go to space and want to
image the earth get a license from our
our division, the commercial remote
sensing regulatory affairs division. and
that implements national security
protections and other um let's say US
equities in terms of licensing those
those activities. Another mission and
the largest certainly by far in terms of
personnel and budget for our office is
space situational awareness. We've
already heard multiple remarks this
morning highlighting the importance of
space traffic management and our office
is in the process of taking over the
public facing space situational
awareness mission from the US Department
of Defense and war for years. The
Department of Defense has provided SSA
information to the public, to space
operators, and to foreign governments
really is sort of a natural outgrowth of
some of the systems they operate for
national security purposes. But during
the first Trump administration, it was
recognized that that's not really a core
national security activity and the
Department of Defense would prefer to
focus on their core mission. So we were
tasked with building out our own system
which now is fully operational and is
onboarding new users as we speak. It's
called tracks the traffic coordination
system for space and it will be um the
US government's premier and primary
public facing for operators and foreign
governments and our own government SSA
system. So we're really excited that
that's happening. You can read about it
all on our website. Um, and as I said,
we have a bunch of operators already
using it, the vast majority of
satellites, and we're onboarding more
users as time goes on. But the third
thing that we do in the office of space
commerce, and this is really, you know,
the team, the team that I lead and what
I want to focus on today is policy
advocacy. And what that means is we sit
inside the US government and we're
really the voice of the private sector.
Our job is to get to know and understand
the needs and goals and frustrations of
industry and then fight to fix those
problems and achieve those goals inside
the US government and externally. So we
spend a lot of time working with other
parts of the US government, working with
the White House, changing US policy,
advocating for things like export
control reform or licensing reforms
across the US government. We also do the
same thing internationally working with
foreign governments trying to advocate
for for example licensing frameworks
that are similar across nations so that
if a comp a company can operate here
it's very easy to operate abroad. One of
the biggest issues right there that
we're working on very deeply is the
European Union Space Act, which for
those of you who don't know is a a very
large proposed law that would unify uh
regulations and laws for commercial
space activities across Europe. If
you're a US company and you want to
provide services in Europe and this act
gets passed, those would be the rules
you'd have to follow. And some of those
rules we have serious problems with.
Some of them are are pretty good. But so
we're engaged with our Department of
State colleagues in a probably years,
certainly monthsl long process of
negotiation and push back and
conversations with European Union
institutions as well as European member
states to try to make sure frankly that
the United States industry continues to
have access to European markets and can
continue to lead as they are right now.
Another issue that we're working on
really is the domestic side of policy,
licensing and regulation. And this I
think is is probably the single most
important if I could you know maybe
maybe speak on behalf of our own office
here. I think it's the single most
important issue in terms of domestic
space policy we're focused on and it's
called mission authorization.
And I'm going to sort of tell you what
this problem is and maybe give a
highlight or a preview of some of the
ways we're going to try to fix it.
The problem frankly is that in some ways
the United States is a victim of our own
success. We have been doing commercial
space things for longer than essentially
any other country in the world. For 50
60 years, there have been two primary
ways that companies could go to space
and then make money down here on Earth.
You could go and do telecommunications
using generally radio frequencies. So
everything from satellite TV, but now
more modern things like Starlink and low
Earth orbit internet enabled
constellations.
or you could go to space and image the
earth and sell those images and data and
products. And you know, the US
regulatory system has responded to that
reality. And we've gotten pretty good at
creating a licensing and policy
structure that makes those business
models work. The FCC, who you'll hear
from right after me, uh has a
well-developed system for licensing
radio frequency usage just like they do
on the Earth. And that industry has
thrived and continues to thrive
obviously with the success of first
Starlink and now Amazon Leo and other
players. My own office um licenses
remote sensing systems as I said and
that industry is also doing quite well.
And that's the system we've built to
deal with those kind of two buckets of
commercial activities. But many of you
in the audience and certainly as we've
heard today and many across the DMV are
trying to do new things and are really
already doing new things. In the past
five or 10 years, industry is looking to
new business models. Everything from
satellite manufacturing, satellite
servicing, lunar surface operations,
asteroid or lunar mining, um data
centers in space using optical
communications, not radio frequencies.
There's there's a whole list uh that
goes on and on. And you'll notice none
of those activities fall in the
traditional categories of sort of
telecom or earth imaging.
And that's great to have new ways to
succeed in space. But it's a problem too
because the US government having built
these legacy systems over decades
frankly doesn't know what to do with
these with these new activities. And
that lack of regulatory clarity where we
essentially don't have any rules or any
way to get to yes on these new
activities makes it harder for these
companies to secure investment because
they can't tell their potential
investors
what the rules will be whether they can
get permission to launch um makes it
harder to get insurance and ultimately
makes it harder to succeed. You know, we
do have these three licenses or excuse
me, three regulators, the FCC, US, and
the FAA that regulate launch and
re-entry, but none of them regulate, for
example, high-powered lasers in space or
space nuclear operations or rendevous
and proximity operations. So, that's a
problem. We need to get to a place where
we can say yes to these companies who
want to do these new activities in
space.
This was recognized as a problem for
years and years. Uh Congress has made
multiple attempts to pass legislation to
solve the problem, fill the gap, get to
a system that can say yes. And all of
those attempts have failed uh for
various reasons basically not having
anything to do with the substance but
having more to do with sort of internal
congressional dynamics.
So recently, last August, the current
administration tasked the Department of
Commerce and in particular the Office of
Space Commerce with solving this
problem. In an August executive order,
we were tasked with developing a
proposal for filling the gap, providing
regulatory clarity for these new some
people call novel space activities,
although some of them aren't that novel
anymore. Some companies have been doing
these for quite a long time. And we've
been working behind the scenes and
sometimes directly with industry since
August uh with a little break for the
shutdown to come up with a proposal for
what this could be, what this could look
like. And I'm excited to say that we are
moments if not days or moments away from
being able to submit that proposal to
the White House and you know seek
approval so that we can actually go out
into the world and implement this thing
and finally solve this problem that has
held industry back for at least a decade
if not more. I don't want to get ahead
of things and I don't want to sort of
get ahead of Secretary Lutnik who's
going to need to approve this proposal
and then ultimately the White House who
will need to as well. So, I'll just give
some high-level previews of what this
could look like, but what we're trying
to do is come up with a certification
process, a very light touch
certification process operated by the
Office of Space Commerce where companies
wanting to do one of these novel
activities that doesn't fit in one of
the traditional categories could submit
an application to us and make a sort of
a barebones light touch set of
commitments. commitments that we would
articulate in advance that they would
need to make to protect US national
security, protect US space operations,
whether it's Department of War or NASA
operations, and some basic commitments
to protect uh the safety in general of
of industry and others who might use
space. If those commitments are made,
then we would grant a certification
after doing a little bit of due
diligence and checking with our inter
agency partners to make sure that
there's no problems that we don't see.
And once that certification is in hand,
which would happen automatically unless
there's a a clear problem within a a
defined time period, then not only could
the company, the applicant sort of be
happy that they have our certification,
but they could actually take that to the
o other regulators, whether it's the FAA
or the FCC, and use that to satisfy at
least portions of those regulatory
systems. That might mean the FCC waving
certain rules not having to do with
radio frequencies, but things about, you
know, debris or end of life missions. We
would have already handled that. So, the
FCC wouldn't need to impose rules on
that. The FAA, which normally conducts a
payload review, well, we would have
already done that, too. So, this could
suffice to, you know, satisfy the
payload review. This is going to take
some time to implement, but the net
result sort of at the end we hope for
novel activities will be more or less a
single-stop shop where they can apply to
us. We have these light touch
commitments that will set out sort of
what good behavior in space looks like
and that's the certification process
they would have to follow. This would
solve the problem in terms of providing
a clear path to yes for industry. It
would also remove potential overlaps and
ambiguity and annoying multiple
processes for all the multiple licenses
that companies have to go through right
now. So like I said, this still is
pending approval and lots of details um
I haven't talked about and will need to
be worked out over time. We hope and we
know this will be a flexible process
where we engage deeply with industry and
our inter agency partners as we figure
this out as we figure out what good
behavior looks like and frankly as we
figure out what a rapid and and easy
certification process looks like sort of
on the the paperwork side of things. But
we're really excited. I think we have an
opportunity now under this
administration and under this guidance
for us to solve this problem and really
enable all of the kinds of activities
you're going to be hearing about here,
heard about yesterday, some of the
workshops, all that new stuff. Um, we
the US government, those of us who work
there, should not be the reason these
activities don't happen. And policy is
something that we can fix. uh we need to
get this problem out of the way so these
businesses can succeed and thrive or not
on their own merits, not because there
is an outdated licensing system in the
United States. So that's the the sort of
top priority in terms of domestic policy
for us. That's what I'm working on and
that's what I wanted to tell you all
about today. So thank you very much and
thanks for having me here.
